title: Submarine cable resilience | APNIC Blog
content:
Skip to the article
Submarine cable resilience
By Geoff Huston on 14 Oct 2026
Category: Tech matters
Tags: Resilience, submarine cable
Share on LinkedIn
Blog home
JaredMcKenzie, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.
The Matsu Islands are an archipelago of 36 islands in the East China Sea, alongside the southeastern coast of mainland China. The islands have been administered since 1949 by Taiwan, part of a larger set of outlying islands administered by Taiwan, which includes the Kinmen and Penghu Islands, which all lie in the Taiwan Strait.
The Matsu Islands are connected to Taiwan’s main island by two submarine cables — Taima No.2, Taima No.3, and soon Taima No.4. The Taiwan Strait is a shallow body of water, with an average depth of 70m. The submarine cables that lie on this seafloor are vulnerable to damage from ship-based activity, like being snagged by fishing equipment or anchors. But these particular cables have been remarkably unlucky. Between 2018 and 2022, the submarine cables between Taiwan and the Matsu Islands were cut 27 times, and there have been four major outages in the three years from 2023 to 2025.
That’s not the only location where submarine cables have suffered many faults. The Baltic Sea is a shallow sea that has a dozen or so submarine communications cables, and undersea electricity and gas pipelines. There have been 11 disruptions to these submarine systems since 2023. Again, a very unlucky track record.
There are an estimated total of 1.5M kilometres of subsea communications cables, used by 607 in-service submarine cable systems (Figure 1) that are critical to the world’s telecommunications services. If they are put out of service for any reason, our satellite systems simply could not replace them. In such a catastrophic scenario, some communities would be totally isolated, with severe logistical and economic ramifications.
Figure 1 — Submarine cables, October 2026. Source: Telegeography.
We regard this collection of submarine cable systems as critical infrastructure for global communication services, and we take care to make them as resilient as possible. Modern warfare can deliberately disrupt communications systems, which adds another source of potential damage to the list of geological and accidental risks facing subsea cables.
On the night of 4 August 1914, days after Britain declared war against Germany, the British cable ship HMTS Alert sailed from Dover into the English Channel. The vessel dragged grappling hooks along the seabed, hauled up five German transatlantic and European telegraph cables, and cut them. This severed Germany’s direct, secure submarine cable links to the Americas, Africa, Spain, and the rest of Europe. Germany was forced to rely on wireless radio transmissions, where British intelligence could readily eavesdrop. If the German cryptography used to protect these wireless communications was broken, then it allowed the British to track military movements and capture critical messages, such as the Zimmermann Telegram.

This same action to deliberately sever undersea cables was repeated by the British in September 1939, cutting German cables to Lisbon and New York.
Protecting the cable
These thin polyester-coated cables at the bottom of the ocean are vulnerable, including to:
Geology in the form of submarine earthquakes or landslips
Being snagged by dragging ship anchors or fishing equipment along the seafloor
Deliberate attacks on the cables with grapnels and cutting equipment
How can cables defend against such risks? The inner core of the fibre optic cables and its copper conductor sheath can be wrapped in additional layers of steel cable jacketing as a form of armour (Figure 2). This is mostly used to reduce its vulnerability to shipping accidents.
Figure 2 — Cross-section of a submarine cable. Source: Telegeography.
Figure 2 is somewhat misleading. What is depicted here is a cross-section of submarine cable used in the segments of the cable that lead to the surface cable station. The cable segments that are laid on the deep-sea floor use just the inner components: Optical fibre and a single thin steel thread wrapped in a silicone gel, surrounded by a copper sheath (used to power the cable repeaters), and wrapped in polyethylene. There are no external armour elements. These deep-sea cable segments are around 20mm in diameter, or the size of a garden hose.
The cable surfaces at a cable landing station. These landing stations are typically plain, secured facilities with reliable power. The preferred location is a coastal point with a low volume of fishing or other maritime traffic, and a steep rise from the deep-sea floor. Cables are at their greatest risk from coastal shipping activity, so the shorter the distance from the deep-sea floor to the cable station on dry land, the better.
Figure 3 — Cable landing station. Source: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 3.0.
Many jurisdictions also declare ‘Cable Protection Zones’ as a warning to marine vessel operators that there are cables on the seafloor in this area, and ships should refrain from fishing activity and anchoring in these areas.
Cable routing
Cable routing is also important in terms of resilience. There are several objectives in a cable route, and not all of them can be optimized at the same time.
The cable route should be as short as possible, as additional cable length raises capital costs and increases end-to-end signal delay.
Cables should avoid areas of active geological activity where possible, such as tectonic plate boundaries and mid-plate rifts. Deeper is better, but within reason. Cables on the floor of a deep ocean section are less vulnerable to shipping activity and hostile efforts to disrupt the cable, but with extreme depths it’s more challenging to locate and raise the cable when undertaking a repair. 
Sometimes there are geographic ‘choke points’ through which many cables are routed. The Bab al-Mandab Strait is not just a choke point for surface vessels passing between the Indian Ocean and the Red Sea, but it is also the conduit through which 16 cables pass (Figure 4). In September 2025, several cables were severed in the Bab al-Mandab Strait, disrupting an estimated 25% of cable capacity between Asia, Europe, and the Middle East. Houthi-controlled waters remain effectively ungovernable for cable protection.
Figure 4 — Cable routes in the Bab al-Mandab Strait. Source: Telegeography.
There is also the Singapore Strait, a major junction for 35 cable systems (Figure 5). This is a shallow water strait that also hosts a significant volume of surface shipping.
Figure 5 — Cable routes in the Singapore Strait. Source: Telegeography.
Further north, between Taiwan and the Philippines is the Luzon Strait, where 18 cables pass (Figure 6). This was the location of an earthquake and a subsequent set of submarine landslides in December 2006 that not only severed all the cables running through this strait, but also buried many of them under deep layers of sediment. It took 11 repair vessels 49 days to bring all the cable systems back into operation.
Figure 6 — Cable routes in the Luzon Strait. Source: Telegeography.
The Black Sea is an area with geopolitical risk and regulatory gaps. While mine risk is confirmed, no cable faults have been directly documented in the war in Ukraine. Russia’s continued presence and the conflict make this region functionally inaccessible for routine cable maintenance.
Geopolitics also plays a role in cable routing. Cable owners will prefer to avoid routes through politically unstable territorial waters if suitable alternative routes exist. There are also political considerations. If a cable lands in US territory, then the cable is subject to several Federal Communications Commission (FCC) constraints, including banning equipment or services from companies the FCC see as a threat to US national security. The FCC has also refused to permit the landing of a cable on US territory if the cable also lands in a territory that the US deems to be a foreign adversary.
Land routes are avoided in general, but there are some circumstances where a land route is the preferred option. Connectivity between Asia and Europe would normally run through the Bab al-Mandab Strait, landing in Egypt in the Gulf of Suez, then overland through Egypt to get to the Mediterranean Sea. There is an alternative route through the Persian Gulf, Iraq and Türkiye, although this entails a segment that transits the Strait of Hormuz, or a second overland segment through Oman and the United Arab Emirates.
Cable faults
Around 200 submarine cable faults are reported worldwide each year, a figure that the International Cable Protection Committee notes has stayed broadly steady in recent years even as the total cable inventory increases. The cables themselves are remarkably reliable. It is the maritime traffic above them that is the cause of most of the problems. 86% of cable faults are likely due to fishing activity or anchoring, and fishing activity is around twice as prevalent as anchoring incidents.
Geological events, such as submarine landslides and seabed movement, account for about 7% of cable faults, cable abrasion for 4%, and component failure (in repeaters) for only 4%.
With the high correlation of faults and maritime activity, it is not surprising that just under one half of cable faults occur in territorial waters, and most of the remainder occur in exclusive economic zones. Just 2% occur on the high seas. Cables are most vulnerable close to shore, in shallow water, where fishing is concentrated, where ships anchor, and where the cable must come ashore at a landing station alongside every other cable serving that coast. The deep ocean, where there is little seabed fishing activity and few ships anchoring, is the safest location for a cable.
National jurisdictions do not stop at the low tide mark of a territory, they extend out into the sea and the seafloor. The 1982 United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (PDF) defined sovereign territorial waters as a 12-mile zone extending out from an economy’s coast. Every coastal economy has exclusive rights to the oil, gas, and other resources in the seabed up to 200 nautical miles from shore or to the outer edge of the continental margin, whichever is the further, subject to an overall limit of 350 nautical miles (650km) from the coast or 100 nautical miles (185km) beyond the 2,500-metre isobath (a line connecting equal points of water depth).
What does this mean for submarine cables? From the point where the cable enters territorial waters, any physical activity related to the cable requires the permission of the authorities. All cable construction and repair operations carried out in these sovereign areas also require the permission of the economy that has exclusive rights to the sea and seafloor.
Location and repair
Locating a cable break is straightforward. An optical pulse will be reflected at the point of a cable break, which can provide the distance to the fault from the start of the cable with considerable precision. At that point, it becomes a marine operation.
A specialist cable repair ship must be engaged, which, in turn, must obtain the relevant government’s permission to work at the location of the cable fault (don’t forget that only 2% of outages occur in international waters). Once at the break location, the repair vessel drags a grapnel along the seabed to hook the cable, cuts it, recovers one end, buoys it off, then recovers the other end. A new section is spliced into the cable aboard the ship in a jointing cabin, the fibre fusion-spliced and tested, the joint rebuilt and sealed against pressure, and the repaired cable laid back down with enough slack to reach the seabed.
The cost of a repair can vary greatly, depending on the location and depth of the fault, the nature of the contracted arrangements for cable repair, the amount of time the cable operator is willing to wait for a repair vessel and crew, and the weather. USD 500k to USD 1M is a representative cost of a single cable repair.
While the number of cables has grown, the time taken to obtain permission to operate repairs in territorial waters has generally increased. Industry data indicates repair response times have more than doubled over the past decade, and the longest single repair recorded in 2023 took 947 days, many of which were spent waiting for permission to undertake the repair.
There is also the issue of repair vessels. The industry has roughly 60 ships capable of repairing a submarine cable, operated under maintenance agreements that pool the cost of running this fleet across cable owners in each geographic region. These collective Submarine Cable Maintenance and Repair Agreements are used in the Atlantic Ocean, the North American Western Coastal region, the Mediterranean, South East Asia and the Indian Ocean, and Yokohama in the North Pacific (Figure 7).
Figure 7 — Areas covered by the five ‘zone’ agreements for pooled submarine cable maintenance and repair. Source: International Cable Protection Committee (PDF).
Analysis by TeleGeography and Infra-Analytics has found that around two-thirds of cable maintenance vessels will reach the end of their service lives by 2040, while total cable kilometres are projected to grow by about 48% over the same period. Closing that gap would take USD 3B and require fifteen replacement ships plus five additional vessels simply to hold current service levels as the submarine cable network expands. The immediate problem is that nobody obviously owns this bill. Cable maintenance is funded through shared agreements that have been optimized for decades to be as cheap as possible, which worked when the fleet was young and is precisely the wrong structure for financing a fleet renewal.
This is the core of the cable resilience problem. Adding cable routes is comparatively easy, because today’s hyperscale cloud companies fund much of the new construction themselves and have strong commercial reasons to do so. However, no individual cable is so critical that it can sustain a business case to operate a dedicated repair fleet. The industry uses pooled resources, which suffer from under-investment.
Investigating cable outages
A rundown of recent cable outages includes:
Subsea cables were damaged in October 2023 by the anchor of the Hong Kong-flagged Newnew Polar Bear operating in the Baltic Sea.
Three cables in the Red Sea were cut in February 2024 by the drifting Rubymar vessel after it was struck by a missile.
The C-Lion1 and the BCS East-West Interlink cables were cut in the Baltic Sea in November 2024 with the Chinese bulk carrier Yi Peng 3 nearby.
Four cables were damaged in December 2024, with anchor drag marks on the Baltic seabed and the Cook Islands-registered tanker Eagle S detained.
Taiwan recorded incidents in January and February 2025 on the Matsu cables.
Three major cables, including SEA-ME-WE 4 and IMEWE, were cut in the Red Sea in September 2025.
Finland and Est

title: How Amazon pushes up prices all across the Internet
content:
October 14, 2026
How Amazon pushes up prices all across the Internet
Amanda Shendruk
Not-Ship turns one next week!! To mark it, I'll be kicking off a campaign for new members. I won't spam you; free subscribers will only get three extra emails on top of the weekly edition.
But first, can I ask for a small birthday present? Hit reply and finish this: I read Not-Ship because...
💙 Amanda
Support Not-Ship!
Last week I wrote about how Amazon's search page is designed to screw you over: the top row trap, the swamp of ads, the discount-washing. Today, I'll explain what's going on behind the scenes, and how Amazon's rules make sure prices stay high not just at Amazon, but everywhere you shop.
In a nutshell, here's what's happening:
This isn't just my theory. This system is at the heart of the US Federal Trade Commission's (FTC) upcoming antitrust case against Amazon.
Let's get into it.
Amazon charges sellers a lot of fees
Amazon relies on independent sellers to populate its online marketplace, and it charges them to be on the site. Amazon takes a big cut. In 2014, this was about 19% of sales. But today, many sellers hand close to half of every sale to Amazon. Half!
Amazon's basic commission (15% of the sale price in most categories) is in line with what eBay and Walmart charge. What pushes Amazon's cut higher are the other fees stacked on top.
Where an Amazon sale goes
Based on an apparel seller that opts for Amazon fulfillment, storage, returns and advertising.
There's the referral fee, which is the commission Amazon takes on every sale. The fulfillment fee is the cost to have Amazon pack and ship items from its warehouses. Then there's advertising: those sponsored spots in the top row we saw in last week's article.
Of these costs, only the referral fee is mandatory. Sellers can choose to ship orders themselves, for example, or forgo advertising. But in practice, the choice isn't actually much of a choice.
Here's what it looks like for a seller considering these so-called options:
In other words, the real choice for sellers isn't between paying for extras or not; it's between making sales or not. The FTC calls Prime eligibility, which effectively requires Amazon's fulfillment service, "a virtual necessity for doing business on Amazon." It says the same of advertising.
So, sellers have to raise prices
Here's where the fees are passed on to us consumers. When sellers give roughly half of their sales to Amazon, the other half isn't profit. That money has to cover making the product, shipping it to Amazon's warehouses, paying staff and everything else. So even if they wanted to absorb Amazon's fees on your behalf, most companies can't afford to. They have to raise their prices.
Don't forget, Amazon's biggest single fee — the referral fee — is a percentage of the price. So when prices go up, Amazon's cut goes up, too.
And they can't charge less elsewhere
Now here's where it gets really crazy. Amazon's Fair Pricing Policy lets it remove the Buy Box (the "Add to Cart" button), or even suspend a seller, if they're offering their item cheaper elsewhere. So, a seller who raises prices on Amazon to cover the fees has to raise them everywhere else too — even on their own website! — or risk losing their Amazon sales.
The consequence is clear: We pay Amazon prices, even when we're not shopping on Amazon.
It's been documented again and again. In 2024, Amazon sellers told CNBC they lost the Buy Box after Target put their products on sale. In an ongoing lawsuit, California's attorney general alleges Amazon pushed brands to get Walmart, Target and other retailers to raise their prices. And when progressive media outlet More Perfect Union reported on this, they even found an Amazon seller who was suspended over a one-cent price gap with Target.
Ideally, market competition would sort this out. High prices send shoppers elsewhere and force fees down. But when sellers can't charge less anywhere else, there's nowhere cheaper to go.
There's no easy way out
For sellers, this is frustrating. So, why don't they just leave? Because Amazon is where the shoppers are: it accounts for about 40% of all US online retail sales. For many sellers, not being on Amazon isn't an option.
At least regulators have noticed. In 2023, the FTC and 17 US states sued Amazon, arguing that it illegally maintains its monopoly power by, among other things, punishing sellers who offer lower prices elsewhere, effectively forcing them to use its warehouses and charging ever-higher fees. Amazon denies any wrongdoing, and the case is set to go to trial next year. In Europe, Germany ordered Amazon to stop controlling its sellers' prices earlier this year, though the decision isn't yet final.
After last week's piece, a Not-Ship reader wrote to say none of this is new: plenty of online stores push ads and fake discounts. That is true. But what's different about Amazon is its reach. When prices increase on Amazon, they tend to increase elsewhere too. You can, of course, choose not to shop on Amazon. But if the FTC is right, you may be paying Amazon's prices anyway.
Calling out capitalism — with data.
Not-Ship's data dispatch. In your inbox, weekly. 
Subscribe
No spam. Just lots of charts. Unsubscribe anytime.
FULL DISCLOSURE
I spent two years working at the Washington Post, which Amazon founder Jeff Bezos owns. During that time, he was busy dismantling the publication, so he wasn't well loved in the newsroom.
CLASSIC ENSHITTIFICATION
In August, I saw Cory Doctorow speak at the Edinburgh International Book Festival. His enshittification concept — the process by which online platforms shift from serving their users to squeezing them — inspired this two-part series on Amazon. If you want to understand it all a lot better, I highly recommend his book Enshittification: Why Everything Suddenly Got Worse and What to Do About It. Somehow it makes antitrust issues both accessible and entertaining!
FROM ELSEWHERE
Here's what I found interesting, important or delightful this week:
Life after death? Alvin Chang's latest masterpiece has dropped! It’s about what people around the world believe happens after we die, drawn from surveys of nearly 130,000 people in 23 countries. (Proud to count Alvin as a Not-Ship subscriber 💙.)
Stunning embroidery. If you haven't seen the work of Irene Saputra, get yourself over to Instagram. Endlessly inspirational.
Instant knowledge. The Ars Notoria was a medieval magic book that promised scholars university learning through prayers, rituals and diagrams. No studying required!

In annual reports, fossil fuel companies have a new playbook for greenwashing
Words are cheap — especially when they’re about the future.

title: Passkeys Are Not a Trap
content:
PASSKEYS
Passkeys Are Not a Trap
SCOTT HELME
14 OCT 2026 • 4 MIN READ
A post called Passkeys are a trap. Do not use them. has been doing the rounds over the last few days, making it pretty high on Hacker News, and I've had it sent to me many times with an 'is this true?' kind of vibe. It's written for "non-technical citizens of the web", and the headline advice is to stop using passkeys and go back to TOTP codes and passwords.
The Argument
The post makes what appears to be one central claim: Passkeys support something called attestation, which lets a website ask for cryptographic proof of what made the passkey.
The author calls this a "hidden dial" and argues that sites will slowly turn it up, until you're only allowed to log in with approved software on an approved operating system, with no modifications, no LineageOS and no sharing your Netflix password. Throw in uBlock Origin, the FIDO Alliance membership list and the UK's image-scanning proposals, and the conclusion is that passkeys are "not designed to prioritize your interests". <that-escalated-quickly.gif>
It's a compelling story. It just doesn't match how any of this actually works...
Your Passkeys Don't Attest
The passkeys most people use are synced passkeys, stored in iCloud Keychain, Google Password Manager, 1Password, Bitwarden or whatever other software of your choosing. These passkeys don't give websites an attestation statement at all, and though a site can ask, what comes back is none. I know this because I wrote an opensource passkeys library and made it available to everyone.
If a consumer website decided tomorrow that it would only accept attested passkeys, it would lock out almost all of its own users, instantly. What website is going to do that? Besides, the guidance for consumer sites has been to not even request attestation for years now.
Attestation Isn't What You Think It Is
The post describes attestation as proving "that an approved passkey manager, operating system, and firmware are in use" which is simply not true.
When it is present, WebAuthn attestation tells the site the make and model of the authenticator, identified by its AAGUID, with a certificate chain from the vendor to back it up. It says nothing about your OS, your browser, your extensions, whether your phone is rooted or jailbroken, your firmware version, or even what colour it is.
The YubiKey Recommendation
This is the part that surprised me the most. For people who want stronger security, the post recommends a hardware security key like a YubiKey, because it "avoids OS-wide attestation".
YubiKeys are the authenticators that do attestation. Every one of them ships with a Yubico-issued attestation certificate, and enterprise attestation exists specifically so organisations can require approved hardware keys. I'd still recommend a YubiKey to anyone who wants one, they're excellent and I use them, but if attestation is the thing you're worried about, the post's own recommendation pushes you towards attestation rather than away from it!
TOTP Is a Step Backwards
The post holds up TOTP as "already" a great solution. TOTP is better than a password alone, absolutely, but it has one big weakness: you can type the code into the wrong website, just ask my good friend Troy Hunt. Phishing kits like Evilginx sit in the middle, relay your password and code to the real site in real time, and walk away with your session. This isn't theoretical, it's how a huge number of account takeovers happen today and we have the evidence to prove it.
This is the problem that passkeys solve. A passkey is bound to the domain it was created for, so your browser simply won't use your example.com passkey on examp1e.com. There's no code to read out and nothing for the user to get wrong. The author even concedes this in the addendum, saying that passkeys are domain-bound and resist man-in-the-middle attacks, but still tells readers to avoid them. Swapping a phishing-resistant credential for a phishable one is a really bad trade...
What You Should Do
Keep using passkeys! Wherever a site offers one, take it, and store it in a password/passkey manager you trust. If you want to be able to move your credentials around, pick a provider that supports that. If you're worried about attestation creeping into consumer logins, then that's worth pushing back on, loudly (if it ever happens). But it hasn't happened, the biggest providers don't support it, and avoiding passkeys today while you wait for it won't protect you from anything, it just leaves you open to phishing.
Sources
I have some experience in this area:
I created WhyNoPasskeys.com to track the availability of passkeys on the Web.
I built and deployed passkeys support on my own SaaS company.
We built our own passkeys library and had it security reviewed.
I wrote about Security considerations when using Passkeys on your website.
I wrote Passkeys 101: An Introduction to Passkeys and How They Work.
I made our passkeys library opensource for everyone to use.
I've done extensive security testing of passkeys implementations.
I've openly acknowledged the limitations of not using attestation on passkeys.
I think most of all that it's important to say I use passkeys everywhere I can because they're currently the best thing we have available to protect our accounts. And they're not a trap.

Live terminal and code previews help show a more realistic view of the terminal, as opposed to the ANSI screenshots used at the GitHub repository. Those are still there, for those who like them.
I would love for you guys to check it out and provide feedback, feature suggestions, whatever!
And a huge thanks to the community of people that have contributed themes, ports to other terminals, and tools to provide conversions between formats over the years.

title: Why is every rationalist blog post way too long? - alex wennerberg
content:
Why is every rationalist blog post way too long?
October 13, 2026
For my piece on Catholic miracle apologetics, I read (correction: skimmed) a 25,000-word post by rationalist blogger Scott Alexander. My piece, which cited (but does not focus on) his, ended up being a cool 2,700 words. I don't think it would benefit from being longer, and it was the result of me cutting around 70% of the text I initially wrote.
Rationalist bloggers do not generally appear to have this impulse. Eliezer Yudkowsky's "sequences" are over one million words long. Nearly every blog post I have read in this ecosystem, even the rare one that contains some good ideas, is painfully long and extremely tedious. These bloggers tend to spend their time on precisely the wrong things, i.e. adding layers of detail and nuance rather than interrogating the one or two assumptions they make at the start or broadening their philosophical background beyond the collection of texts popular within their subculture.
It seems to me that, in this community, verbosity is a substitute for thoroughness: surely, if someone wrote a lot about something, and is able to demonstrate that by producing a large volume of text, they must have something worthwhile to say about it? Consider when blogger Gwern explained that nicotine, actually, is not addictive, and is good for you, as long as you don't smoke it, over the course of 9,000 words, with over 100 references. It turns out, actually, nicotine is addictive, and is bad for you even if you don't smoke it, as you probably already obviously knew.
In any case, what is missing from this endlessly verbose rationalist writing style is wisdom. Wisdom involves discretion: an intuition for what ideas are and are not worth seriously pursuing, and the ability to determine what does and does not need to be said. This community, broadly speaking, does not seem to value wisdom as a trait at all; the idea that something may be true, valuable, or good merely because it is common sense or inherited tradition is anathema to them. Instead, there is a heavy bias towards that which is unconventional and counterculture, with the amount of ink spilled for heterodox ideas taken as evidence in itself that these ideas are worth taking seriously.

title: Suicide rates highest ever among middle-aged men
content:
Suicide rates highest ever among middle-aged men
Those aged 50 to 54 are at greatest risk of taking their own lives as charities warn deaths ‘remain stubbornly high’
Michael Searles
Deputy Health Editor.
Ben Butcher
Data Editor
Updated 13 October 2026 5:22pm BST
Published 13 October 2026 5:05pm BST
139
Gift this article free
Add us as preferred source
Suicide rates among middle-aged men are higher than ever, new figures have revealed.
Men in their early 50s were more likely to die by suicide than anyone else last year, according to data from the Office for National Statistics.
There were also increases in suicides among pensioners, with the biggest rise among those aged 75 and older, while the rates among men under 45 fell slightly.
Mark Winstanley, the chief executive of Rethink Mental Illness, said the rate of deaths by suicide remained “stubbornly high”.
He said: “Every suicide is a devastating tragedy, and these figures are a stark reminder that many people are reaching crisis point without getting the help they need.”
The reasons behind suicide were “complex”, he said, but added that many people were “facing significant pressures in their lives, including financial issues, job insecurity, rising housing costs, loneliness and poor mental health”.
Suicide rate highest on record
Mr Winstanley added: “While these factors affect everyone differently, they can contribute to distress and overwhelm, and leave people at risk of suicide.”
The data, which cover England and Wales, showed that 6,162 suicide deaths had been registered in 2025. This was down from 6,190 last year, but the overall rate remained broadly the same at 11.3 deaths per 100,000 people.
The stats watchdog uses deaths per 100,000 people to calculate changing rates while accounting for changes in the size of the population.
Almost a third of the deaths were among men aged 45 to 64, which was up by 49 compared with 2024. The rate increased to 23.8 per 100,000, up from 23.2 the year before and the highest on record since data collection began in 1981.
Advertisement
For men aged 50 to 54 specifically, the rate increased to 28, suggesting this group was at the highest risk.
Men continued to be more than three times as likely to take their own lives as women overall. Among middle-aged women, there were 553 deaths – a rate of seven per 100,000, which was the same as 2024.
Sonya Trivedy, the executive director of external engagement at Samaritans, said the figures “show that suicide rates are among the highest recorded rates this century”.
She said: “The evidence is clear that successive governments have failed to deliver on their promise to reduce suicide rates and make suicide prevention a priority. Today must act as a wake up call. The current approach is not working; we need meaningful action and proper funding if lives are to be saved.”
The data show a growing gap in suicide rates between middle-aged men and those aged 25 to 44.
RECOMMENDED
Simon Reeve: 'I was a whisker away from taking my own life'
Read more
There were 19.5 deaths per 100,000 men aged 25 to 44 last year, which is the widest gap since 2009, when middle-aged male suicide rates overtook those of younger adults. The rate increased from 14 to 14.4 per 100,000 for those aged 65 to 74 and from 13.2 to 15.4 among those aged 75 or older.
Marjorie Wallace, the chief executive of mental health charity Sane, said she was “not surprised” by the data. She said: “Analysis of the contact we receive reflects this – almost 60 per cent of our callers now talk about suicide or self-harm, a very different picture than 10 years ago.
“While middle-aged men in their forties and fifties still remain at greatest risk, our other concern is the number of young people, particularly girls and women aged 16 to 24, who report anxiety and depression on a scale not experienced before.”

title: Things to know if you get cancer (2026 Edition) · JJ Maxwell
content:
index
Things to know if you get cancer (2026 Edition)
2026.10.14
I was diagnosed with squamous cell carcinoma in my mouth in May 2026. Here are some things I learned based on that experience so far.
You need to be doggedly persistent on scheduling things. Yes this means lots of phone calls. If you get an appointment a few weeks out, call back a few days later and ask for something sooner and see if they have any cancellations. I could only get an appointment 4 weeks out with an ENT (this was before I knew anything was wrong). My wife made me call back and I was able to get in that week due to a cancellation.
AIs may downplay the seriousness of things. I was chatting with various models and most pushed me in the direction of “you don’t have cancer” for a while. Just something to note.
You may need to push for comprehensive genetic testing. Some doctors were weird about this and didn’t order it promptly, even after telling me they would. My surgeon, who told me he’d get it done, eventually referred me out to an oncologist. This caused a multi-month delay to getting genetic results, since the first results were done on the surgery tumor, not the biopsy tumor. No one cares more about your case than you, so take control and send lots of follow-ups.
You can find the “Standard of Care” flow charts for every cancer type. Look and get through this yourself to see what the options are based on how things have progressed. NCCN guidelines. You may need to make an account, which you can do as a non-professional. I like the PDF files. They also have an interactive navigator. Use AI to help you figure out what to pick based on your case.
If surgery is recommended, I would try and talk to someone who has undergone the surgery. I did not do this and regret it. Ask them how intense things were, what it felt like, etc. My surgeon talked me through my surgery, but it was a lot rougher on me physically than I expected. Ask the surgeon how many of these surgeries they do a year and what the complication rate is.
Get a second opinion as soon as possible, no matter how much you like your plan. This may require a lot of calling and getting on an airplane, but I’d move to schedule it at a top cancer center as soon as you are relatively sure of your diagnosis. Ask for a second read of the pathology at the center where you get the second opinion.
I started a new folder on my Mac, and after appointments I’d dictate what happened and what the doctor said and have the AI make a new document summarizing things and asking its own follow-up questions for next time. Nice to be able to refer to this over time.
Check out all the resources and materials at the Sijbrandij Foundation. Sid (GitLab cofounder) took matters into his own hands when standard of care ran out. Schedule a call with these guys. They are great and have good materials and questions to ask your doctors.
Note, since this is on the front page of Hacker News right now. exhilaration suggested that if you are within a 2-3 hour drive of a major cancer center, go there instead of your local community hospital. Use the US News cancer hospital rankings. The top centers usually take your insurance, so use vacation days and book a hotel if you have to. The largest benefit I saw was speed. At MD Anderson I got a question answered within 20 minutes of a visit, because the doctor called the pathologist who he was on a first name basis with. If that wasn’t at a cancer center, it would have taken days, or more likely the question never would have been answered at all (I had asked my oncologist about this and he’d just shrugged). The rest of the HN comments are worth reading too.

title: Future of Cancer Care Today — Sijbrandij Foundation LLC
content:
There is more science available to cancer patients than what one care team can keep up with. New diagnostics, treatments, trials, and suppliers keep emerging, and when standard of care runs out, patients are usually left to figure out what else might be possible on their own.
Future of Cancer Care Today is not a medical provider. We do not diagnose, prescribe, or direct treatment. We provide a non-clinical support layer focused on information, education, and decision support, intended to complement your relationship with your care team. Some materials may be generated with the support of artificial intelligence and should be reviewed with your medical providers before informing any care decisions. All decisions regarding your care belong to you and your doctor.
DIRECTOR, PATIENT CONNECTIONS
Bayli is a scientist and science communicator dedicated to improving the lives of those diagnosed with cancer. She developed her expertise in cancer immunotherapy research at the University of Florida and in translating complex scientific findings into accessible language during her time at the American Brain Tumor Association. Bayli was also a fellow at the National Institutes of Health, Office of the Director, through the American Association for the Advancement of Science Science and Technology Policy Fellowship, where she addressed policy needs related to incorporating the public into clinical research and bioethical issues. Inspired by her mother's diagnosis with metastatic colon cancer, she now applies her caregiving, scientific, and communication expertise to provide information and compassion to clients of FCCT.
LinkedIn Profile →
ASSOCIATE, PATIENT INFORMATION
Donnia is a scientist with training in chemistry, public health, and pharmaceutical sciences. Before joining FCCT, she was an Early Stage Researcher in the AGePOP consortium, an EU Horizon 2020 program focused on medicines for special populations, including older adults. At FCCT, Donnia supports patient case research, resource mapping, and preparation of educational materials for patients.
NEW
One standing authorization for records, imaging, data, and tissue.
LEARN MORE
USE OR REVIEW THE RELEASE
Identifies who is authorizing the release and where the materials are held. The form includes the patient’s information, the authority of any personal representative, and multiple releasing institutions and departments.
Defines the records and data covered. This includes medical and billing records; laboratory, pathology, and imaging reports; original imaging files; electronic health information exports; genomic and laboratory reports; raw data files; and related assay and analysis information. The authorization covers all dates.
Includes available tissue and other specimens. Covered materials include pathology slides and tissue blocks, as well as blood, plasma, serum, bone marrow, and other biological materials.
Addresses sensitive information separately. The patient must initial the categories they authorize for release, including genetic or genomic, HIV/AIDS-related, mental health, and reproductive or sexual health information. Psychotherapy notes are excluded. Substance use disorder records covered by 42 C.F.R. Part 2 require separate consent.
Defines who may receive the materials. The authorization covers specified healthcare, laboratory, data exchange, and research recipients, as well as another person or organization identified by the patient. The recipient may tell the releasing institution where to send the materials.
Creates a standing authorization. Once the form is on file, an authorized recipient may request covered materials without obtaining a new patient signature for each request. The authorization remains effective for up to 99 years unless the patient revokes it or applicable law requires an earlier expiration.
Explains the limits of releasing physical materials. Tissue and other specimens can be released only when they remain available and release is permitted. Materials that were discarded or not preserved cannot be recovered. A release may also reduce what remains for future care or testing.
Includes standard authorization terms. These address purpose, expiration, revocation, possible re-disclosure, voluntariness, permitted fees, the right to a copy, governing law, and signatures. The form is intended to satisfy HIPAA authorization requirements under 45 C.F.R. § 164.508.
Materials move directly from the holder to the patient or chosen recipient. FCCT does not receive or store data or tissue and does not provide legal or medical advice.
If our work could be useful to you or your community, please reach out. There is no cost to patients or families for our help.
PATIENTS AND CAREGIVERS
Whether you are newly diagnosed, facing progression, or trying to figure out what comes next, we may be able to help you think more clearly about the path ahead.
CLINICIANS, RESEARCHERS, PARTNERS
If you are working in diagnostics, therapeutics, personalized medicine, or health technology, and believe patients need better support navigating complexity, let's talk about how our work could complement yours.
FUNDERS
Future of Cancer Care Today is incubated by the Sijbrandij Foundation, and grew out of Sid Sijbrandij's cancer journey and lessons learned from the many other patients and families we work with.

Jev: For The Builders AND Dreamers
Oct 14, 2026
TL;DR: We're releasing an improved Jev 1.14.0 along with experimental features for our dreamers: images, a new type, and longer context. Enter the danger zone at your own risk. 🔥
Our Philosophy
A huge debate we’ve been having is on the balance between reliability and creativity.
To really care about the prod builders, we should be shipping models that meet our quality bar for intelligence and have been battle-tested to the limits of what we can do internally.
On the other hand, there’s no way that our team has a full understanding of what is needed to spark delight in the world and build sick sci-fi. We don’t want to impose our values of extreme reliability on those dreamers.
Our solution: share those dreamer-ready features under “danger zone” flags in our API headers. These are features that will be here to stay for future models, are (as far as we can tell) better than what exists out there, and will continue to get better by leaps and bounds. But as a warning, we think there is still way too much jaggedness for us to vouch for these for production use cases!
See these new capabilities as a continuation of what we’ve built over 2 years of stealth. They’re less ready for automation, but very fun to play with. They’re also an early glimpse into what we’re focused on making reliable enough to meet TypeSafe standards.
Composable Images
Not only are we enabling multimodality for future Jev models, we’re enabling it for the current Jev that you all know and love. Surprise: the Jev you all know and love (jev-1.13.0) was multimodal all along!
Image support is fully composable via a find-and-replace in assets. You can put them anywhere that our JSON interface supports: in the state, instructions, or even criteria! Play around with it, push the boundaries of technology, and let us know where Jev can improve.
As a warning, all models (Jev included) perform worse on multimodality over pure text. Breaking down questions into the simplest possible decompositions helps a lot.
TypeSafe-Danger-Zone-Images: true
Check out docs: docs.typesafe.ai/go/images
Types Beyond Decisions
We’re introducing another new type as well: box. It returns a single bounding box - no type errors allowed. It’s our first type that’s not purely meant for smart-if statements, and is a preview for our explorations beyond simple decisions into what else System One Models can support.
We made huge leaps and bounds on this one recently, so we’re enabling this only for jev-1.14.0 (spoilers).
Check out docs: docs.typesafe.ai/go/box
Size does matter, apparently 💅
We’ve heard you loud and clear on context lengths. Jev actually supports a much longer context length than we’ve enabled in production. We chose to limit it intentionally because Jev, like all models, is less reliable on longer contexts, and this constraint encourages more effective usage patterns in prod.
We aren’t your parents though, so while we strongly recommend limiting context length, you no longer have to:
TypeSafe-Danger-Zone-Long-Context: true
Check out docs: docs.typesafe.ai/models#context-length
Opt-in to help us
We love the community’s desire to help make models better! We’ve added an opt-in to allow you to help find model jaggedness with your queries. We will still not train on your queries, but this does make it easier for us to find issues and help debug your use cases.
Jev-1.14.0
We’re also releasing a new version of Jev under jev-preview! Not meant to be flashy but instead be small, subtle improvements to everything. Most things should be a tiny bit better, but we expect the largest gain in multi-lingual support.
Model releases should generally also be strict improvements, but we’re well aware of how much developers hate updating their dependencies. jev-latest will be updated to jev-1.14.0 in a week. jev-1.13.0 will be available for a while. 
We intend to give 60 days warning before jev-1.13.0 is formally deprecated, and 30 days for jev-1.14.0. We’ll release a deprecation policy prior to this.
Measuring Intelligence
As you all know, we dislike public benchmarks. However, we have our own internal best guesses on how to measure the form factor of intelligence that matters most for developers. 
We’re trying something new out here: we’re going to treat you guys like adults and share this with you all.
Some nuance
This measurement is our best guess and will continue to evolve. If ever we show you our internal numbers again, don’t expect them to be consistent.
Don’t believe it entirely. Always favor your own experimentation and evals with your use cases.
We’re including only open weight models because we guard our validation set very closely and are spooked out about the data policies of our model providers.
This is likely biased towards our models. Feel free to ignore our model, and instead focus on the relative ranking of open source models.

What’S Next
Lots of people love to ask what kind of sci-fi we’re releasing next. While we are working on some mindblowing stuff, expect most releases to be beautifully boring (like we think AI should be): small improvements across the board, better stability, and features for real deployment.

title: LFM2.5-24B-A2B: Built for Fast On-Device Agents | Blog | Liquid AI
content:
NEWS
/
MODELS
LFM2.5-24B-A2B: Built for Fast On-Device Agents
OCT 13, 2026
ON THIS PAGE
What changed since LFM2-24B-A2B
Benchmarks
Fast inference everywhere
Run local agents with LFM2.5-24B-A2B
Get Started
Citation
Today, we release LFM2.5-24B-A2B, a 24B-parameter reasoning model with just 2B active parameters, built for fast, private agents on-device. It is the largest and final model in the LFM2.5 family, which now spans two orders of magnitude: from LFM2.5-230M to LFM2.5-24B-A2B.
LFM2.5-24B-A2B is competitive with Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, a model with ~50% more total and active parameters, on five of eight agentic and tool-use benchmarks, scoring 48.09 on LiveClaw versus 38.19 and 27.69 on AutomationBench versus 8.72.  Because only 2B parameters are active per token, it runs up to 1.7× faster than comparable MoEs on-device, with 184 tokens/s on an Apple M5 Max and up to 21K output tokens/s on a single NVIDIA B300 GPU.
The base (LFM2.5-24B-A2B-Base) and post-trained (LFM2.5-24B-A2B) models are open-weight and available today on Hugging Face and our Playground. Check out our docs on how to run and fine-tune it locally.
What changed since LFM2-24B-A2B
LFM2.5-24B-A2B builds on our previous LFM2-24B-A2B release, with an expanded vocabulary and context window, scaled-up pretraining, and large-scale reinforcement learning. Unlike its predecessor, LFM2.5-24B-A2B is a reasoning-only model that produces an explicit chain of thought before its final answer. We adopted this strategy to leverage its high decode speed and improve answer quality.
Architecture. It keeps the 40 layers, 64 experts per MoE block with top-4 routing, and the same hybrid of gated short convolutions and GQA. The two architectural changes are the context window extension from 32,768 to 131,072 tokens, and the in-place tokenizer expansion, which doubles the vocabulary from 65K to 128K tokens for better non-Latin tokenization.
Pre-training was scaled up from 17T tokens to 33T tokens.
Mid-training has two phases. The first runs 2T tokens at 32K context on curated, higher-quality data weighted toward reasoning, math, code, instruction following, and multilingual text. The second runs 300B tokens at 131K context, weighted toward long context data. Tool calls and multi-turn trajectories appear throughout both phases to prepare the model for agentic workloads.
Post-training turns LFM2.5-24B-A2B-Base into the agentic LFM2.5-24B-A2B in a five-stage pipeline as illustrated below: (1) Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), (2) Teacher Specialization, (3) non-agentic and (4) agentic Multi-Domain On-Policy Distillation (MOPD), and (5) Agentic Reinforcement Learning (Agentic RL), training the model inside agent harnesses, such as OpenClaw, Hermes Agent, Pi, and OpenCode.
Figure 2: LFM2.5-24B-A2B Post-training recipe
During teacher specialization, LFM2.5-24B-A2B exhibited well-known reward-hacking behaviors: searching for the final answer in a repository's git history or on platforms like GitHub, PyPI, and Hugging Face. More surprisingly, it even figured out it was in a sandbox, as shown in the examples below.
This behavior looks emergent but might be explained by training data containing similar patterns. We tightened our sandboxes in response, and all reported results below come from sealed evaluation environments.
Benchmarks
We evaluated LFM2.5-24B-A2B across 16 benchmarks covering tool use and agentic workflows, knowledge, instruction following, math, and coding. Despite being the smallest model in total and active number of parameters, it is competitive with, and often outperforms, larger MoEs with ~50% more total and active parameters, such as Qwen3.6-35B-A3B.

Table 1: LFM2.5-24B-A2B benchmark performance*.
LFM2.5-24B-A2B leads or matches the competition on five of the eight tool-use and agentic benchmarks (AutomationBench, BFCLv4, ToolSandbox, LiveClaw, and τ³-Bench Banking), with its widest margin on AutomationBench, where it scores more than three times the next-best model. It also leads on all three instruction-following benchmarks. Larger models keep an edge on knowledge-heavy benchmarks like GPQA Diamond, HLE, and AA-Omniscience, and on coding benchmarks like SWE-Bench Verified (OpenCode) and SciCode.
The results make LFM2.5-24B-A2B an ideal foundation for agents that need to reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device. For knowledge-heavy workloads, we recommend pairing LFM2.5-24B-A2B with retrieval or web search, which plays to its tool-calling strength.
Fast inference everywhere
LFM2.5-24B-A2B ships with day-one support across the inference ecosystem:
llama.cpp — GGUF checkpoints for efficient edge inference
MLX — Optimized inference for Apple Silicon
vLLM — GPU-accelerated serving for production throughput
SGLang — High-performance GPU serving framework
ONNX — Cross-platform inference across diverse accelerators
All runs were collected on Pipette, the same benchmarking infrastructure behind Liquid AI's public device performance data.
Edge inference. Due to the efficient LFM2 architecture, LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest of the compared MoEs at reading in prompts and generating answers. It decodes 184 tokens/s on an Apple M5 Max and 114 tokens/s on an AMD Ryzen AI Max+ 395, up to 1.7x faster than the next-best model, while using the least memory.
GPU inference. To demonstrate the competitiveness of LFM architecture we compare the GPU inference throughput to other similarly sized MoE models. We measure GPU throughput (total output tokens / wall time) on a single NVIDIA B300 GPU using a sustained-load setting: at each concurrency level, we continuously maintain the target number of in-flight requests, replacing each completed request immediately.
We benchmark each model with SGLang 0.5.22, 1,024 input tokens, up to 256 output tokens, in BF16. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest model in its size class, reaching over 21K output tokens per second at high concurrency.
Run local agents with LFM2.5-24B-A2B
LFM2.5-24B-A2B’s size, speed, and capabilities make it a great choice for agents that run continuously on your own hardware. In the demo below, we run it inside Hermes Agent on an M5 Max MacBook Pro, where it plans, calls tools, and works through a real task entirely on-device, without any cloud API calls.
Video 1: Local Hermes Agent with LFM2.5-24B-A2B creating a morning briefing about trending models on Hugging Face and responding to follow up questions.
The point of the demo is not the individual tools. It is that the tool-dispatch loop feels interactive on consumer hardware: ask, propose, confirm, run, repeat, all in well under a second per dispatch, with full audit trails and your data never leaving the device. Check out our local agent guide for how to serve the model locally and connect it with the agent harness of your choice.
Get Started
Start building today with LFM2.5-24B-A2B, available on Hugging Face.
For API inference, you can also sign up for Liquid Console where you'll receive $2 in credit to get started. The model is priced at $.10/1M input tokens (at $.05 for cached input) and $1.00/1M output tokens.
With LFM2.5, we're delivering on our vision of AI that runs anywhere. These models are:
Open-weight — Download, fine-tune, and deploy. See our model license.
Fast from day one — Native support for llama.cpp, MLX, and vLLM across Apple, AMD, Qualcomm, and Nvidia hardware
A complete family — From base models for customization to specialized audio and vision variants, one architecture covers diverse use cases
We can't wait to see what you build.
Download on Hugging Face
Run your harness of choice locally with LFM2.5-24B-A2B
Integrate with our API

title: Americans’ Social Activity Has Steeply Declined in the Past 30 Years
content:
Americans’ Social Activity Has Steeply Declined in the Past 30 Years
In recent years, there has been extensive discussion of a social decline in the United States, including a U.S. surgeon general advisory in 2023 that declared American loneliness to be an “epidemic.”
Various surveys have tracked America’s social decline over the past few decades. Tracking data from the American Time Use Survey shows that Americans are spending more time alone and less time with friends than they were two decades ago. Perhaps most notably, the American Perspectives Survey has found that from 1990 to 2021, the percentage of Americans with five or more close friends dropped by 25 points, from 63% to 38%.
But while extensive public tracking data show general declines in Americans’ socialization, little, if any, public data show what this looks like for the average American — how the day-to-day activities Americans participate in have changed over the past few decades.
In a new survey, Data for Progress surveyed 1,098 U.S. adults and asked them how many times they engaged in various specific social activities in the past 12 months. These questions directly replicate the DDB Needham Life Style surveys, which tracked Americans’ participation in various activities from 1975-1999 and were referenced in Robert Putnam’s 2000 book “Bowling Alone.” In this analysis, Data for Progress’ 2026 data is compared with the DDB Needham Life Style survey from 1995, which is the earliest year in which full data for all comparison questions was available.
This survey finds significant, double-digit declines in Americans’ participation in key social activities from 1995 to 2026. 
The chart below compares the percentage of Americans who report participating in each tested activity at least one time in the past 12 months, between the 1995 and 2026 surveys. We find that Americans’ participation in various social activities has declined by double-digit margins, including attending a class or seminar (-22), entertaining people in your home (-21), attending church or a place of worship (-20), going on a picnic (-19), going to a club meeting (-19), playing cards (-19), going out to breakfast at a restaurant (-13), and doing volunteer work (-12).
A few activities have seen increased engagement: using the internet (+90), playing a home video game (+22), attending an exercise class (+14), going to a pop or rock concert (+13), and taking an airline trip for personal reasons (+5).
Methodology note: This analysis compares two surveys conducted using different methodologies, including differences in constructing sampling frames, modes, and weighting approaches. The findings below should be read as suggestive of trends, not a precise estimate of change. Please see the “Methodology” section below for more information.
One of the steepest declines in the survey is for “entertaining people in my home.” While in 1995, 88% of Americans reported entertaining others at home at least once in the past year, this number has declined to 67% in 2026.
Church attendance has dropped from 74% in 1995 to 54% in 2026.
The percentage of Americans who report having gone on a picnic in the past year has declined from 58% in 1995 to 39% in 2026.
There has also been a 19-point decline in attendance at club meetings, from 45% in 1995 to 26% in 2026.
This analysis adds to existing public data on America’s social decline. Previous reports have found that Americans are spending less time with others and reporting fewer close friends. This new analysis demonstrates that Americans are indeed spending less time in specific social settings, such as restaurants, churches, picnics, parties, bars, and social clubs.
Methodology
The DDB Needham survey was conducted by Market Facts using a stratified quota sampling procedure that begins with a sampling frame acquired from commercial list brokers. The sample oversamples by demographics such as race, gender, and marital status to oversample lower propensity respondents. Finally, the survey contacted individuals via mail.
In comparison, the Data for Progress adult sample was conducted through web panel suppliers and ensured national representativeness via quota fielding and post-stratification weighting.
There is plenty of research on the compositional differences that exist across survey collection modes, and this is likely to affect these results as questions about religiosity and loneliness tend to demonstrate modal differences and social desirability biases. We understand that these factors are at play in our comparison, but find that the magnitude and consistency in trends across measures is a substantial signal about trends in behaviors nonetheless.  
SEPTEMBER 29, 2026

title: It took me nine years to hack my Xbox 360 – Kennedn's Blog
content:
I purchased a Matrix CoolRunner Rev D back in 2017. This little chip is called a glitcher and it’s a type of modchip. Its sole purpose, the reason it was designed, is to deliver a short pulse of energy (~ 100 nanoseconds) to an Xbox 360 Console.
You might ask yourself, “What’s the point in that?”. The answer is quite interesting.
Microsoft are good at security
It boils down to the simple fact that Microsoft learned from the mistakes of their previous console (the original Xbox) and designed security well on their successor.
So well in fact, that it was deemed essentially unhackable by conventional approaches:
tmbinc said it himself, software based approaches of running unsigned code on the 360 mostly don’t work, it was designed to be secure from a software point of view. 1
The entry point for the system, dubbed 1BL, is physically baked into the silicon of the Xbox 360’s CPU 2. The job of 1BL is to load the next phase of the bootloader, called CB from flash storage, and verify that it was signed by Microsoft.
So without Microsoft’s signing keys, there was no real way to hijack control of the system during the boot process. And it only becomes harder as the console boots up through its different phases. Additional security features are turned on as it cascades up the boot chain. And they would all need individually circumvented to get any code running on the console that Microsoft haven’t been over with a fine toothed comb.
So if the door to the castle is locked, and the guards, who are wise to equine ploys, are checking ID at the door, how does one get in? Well you don’t use a key. You inform the guard that his shoelaces are untied and hit him over the head with a club.
Finding the weak link
The point is that if the lock itself is secure, and the procedures surrounding entry are sound, sometimes the weakest link becomes something more fundamental. In our metaphor this is a person, but in the case of the Xbox 360, it is the fact that computation relies on stable energy conditions to behave in a predictable manner.
And this is the idea that fault injection subverts. In the case of the Xbox 360, researchers found that by very quickly toggling a reset signal on the CPU (CPU_RESET), a signal that is usually supposed to reinitialise the CPU, something far more interesting happened. Instead of resetting, the CPU executed the current instruction incorrectly.
Graph demonstrating glitching as voltage over time 3.
This gave the researchers a very useful primitive. They found that an instruction integral to the signature verification process, the mr (move register) instruction, could be glitched into ignoring a value it was about to move and instead move a 0 into its destination register 4.
So by simply knowing when, and toggling the lights on and off, they gained arbitrary code execution.
The future is glitching
It is astounding to me that this kind of esoteric side channel exists at all. But I think the larger point is that it’s becoming more common.
The sort of trust chains that made the Xbox 360 hard to hack 10 years ago have now become commonplace in the world of computing hardware. Microsoft themselves began enforcing hardware backed secure boot for their Operating Systems back in 20215.
More recently in 2024, the security features of an ESP32 v3 (secure boot and flash encryption) were bypassed using a fault injection attack 6.
And there are recent examples specifically leveraging the Raspberry Pi Pico Microcontroller to perform similar fault injection attacks
Apple AirTag’s firmware was dumped in 2021 by stacksmashing using a Raspberry Pi Pico and fault injection 7.
The PicoFly modchip, released in 2023 for the Nintendo Switch, uses fault injection to defeat secure boot on the console 8.
To me, this suggests that fault injection has become a more attractive attack vector in recent years due to a security ecosystem that has hardened over time. But I think it has in turn also become more accessible than ever, with the advent of cheap and accurate microcontrollers such as the Pi Pico.
A love letter to the Pico
The Raspberry Pi Pico microcontroller, released in 2021 for £5 by the Raspberry Pi Foundation 9.
The Pico itself is versatile because it allows for very precise timing via its PIO blocks. These specialised blocks come with enough primitives to implement many standard protocols and have an effective timing resolution of ~7.5 nanoseconds due to the 133 MHz clock 10:
133 MHz
1
≈7.52ns
I have seen this versatility myself first hand when I finally dusted off the Matrix CoolRunner in 2026 and decided to take another crack at modchipping my Xbox 360.
Back in 2017, when I bought the thing, it was quite expensive to modchip an Xbox 360. You needed a number of tools and skills to successfully mod one:
A glitching chip
Solder and an iron
A NAND programmer
A JTAG programmer
I tried to save some money by building my own NAND / JTAG programmer using the printer port (LPT port) on a very old PC that I had in reserve for the specific purpose. If I had ever got this working it would have taken over 30 minutes to dump the NAND. I do not recall the reason but I did not manage to pull this off in 2017 and the project was shelved.
LPT NAND dumper wiring diagram 11.
Reattempting this same procedure in 2026 was a breeze by comparison. I was able to flash PicoFlasher onto a Pi Pico and solder it to the correct pads on my Xbox 360. The dump operation then only took a handful of seconds to run.
Raspberry Pi Pico wired to the NAND interface header on the Xbox 360.
Similarly I flashed Pico-dirtyJTAG onto a Pi Pico and was able to program the CoolRunner’s timing files using Octal450’s Timing Files and installing the urjtag project from source.
Raspberry Pi Pico wired to Matrix CoolRunner JTAG interface.
Summary
So, even the most carefully crafted tower can collapse under the weight of its own fundamental assumptions. Like many aspects of computer security, fault injection has become a game of cat and mouse, with increasingly sophisticated defences being met by new tools and methods of circumventing them.
But I think we have now reached a point where DIY tooling has really begun to shine, making light work of challenges that, just a decade ago, required expensive, specialised equipment.
And I have seen this first hand, a project that defeated me in 2017 was made trivial in 2026 by a £5 microcontroller.
Funnily enough, a software-only exploit for the Xbox 360 dropped just last week , rendering my years of effort somewhat moot. Nevertheless, it was a fascinating deep dive into the inner workings of the console and the security mechanisms designed to protect it.
